tip: 'Chiunque' (whoever) normally takes the subjunctive: 'chiunque parli italiano', not 'chiunque parla'.
'Stavo leggendo' (I was reading) sets the ongoing background; 'è caduta la luce' reports the sudden event.
Here 'lo' stands for a whole idea, not a masculine noun: 'non lo so' means I don't know it (the fact).
With 'stare' plus a gerund, the reflexive pronoun can sit before 'stare': 'ti stai divertendo'.
'Ne' replaces a counted noun already understood: 'quanti ne vuoi' means how many of them do you want.
'Fidarsi' pairs with 'di' for the person trusted: 'ci fidiamo di te' means we trust you.
Many '-ire' verbs add '-isc-' inside the present tense: 'trasferirsi' becomes 'si trasferisce'.
Italian usually keeps the garment singular even for several people: 'si tolgono il cappotto', one coat each.
'Da' plus a present-tense verb marks ongoing time: 'conosco da anni' means I have known her and still do.
'Parlare' takes 'di', and 'ne' replaces that 'di' phrase: 'ne abbiamo parlato' means we talked about it.
'Fallo' is the short command 'fa'' (do) plus 'lo' (it): the pronoun attaches to the end of the command.
Before another pronoun, 'vi' becomes 've': 've la racconto' means I tell it to you.
Actions people do to each other take 'essere' in the past, and the ending agrees: 'ci siamo incontrati'.
For a polite 'Lei' command, use the subjunctive form: 'parli', not 'parla', in 'parli più lentamente'.
The informal 'tu' command of an '-are' verb ends in '-a': 'tu parla', while 'tu parli' is the plain present.
The reflexive pronoun attaches to the end of an infinitive and matches the subject: 'vestirsi' becomes 'vestirmi'.
'Dare su' means to look out onto: 'la finestra dà sul giardino' overlooks the garden.
Here 'da' means through or via, not from: 'il treno passa da Bologna' goes by way of Bologna.
Here 'per' plus an infinitive means in order to: 'per comprare una casa' means in order to buy a house.
'Da' before a time word can mean starting from: 'da domani' means from tomorrow onward.
'Potrebbe' is the polite could form of 'potere', used for courteous requests: 'potrebbe spiegarlo di nuovo?'.
Italian keeps 'che' even when English drops the word that: 'le persone che conosco' means the people I know.
Each reflexive verb needs its own pronoun: 'ci svegliamo', 'ci vestiamo', one 'ci' per verb.
'Benché' (although) takes the subjunctive: 'benché faccia freddo', not 'fa freddo'.
'Prendine' is 'prendi' (take) plus 'ne' (of them): 'prendine un altro' means take another one of them.
'Credo che' (I believe that) triggers the subjunctive: 'faccia bel tempo', not 'fa'.
English drops the pronoun in 'the house I live in', but Italian must keep it: 'la casa in cui vivo'.
With 'stare' plus a gerund, the pronoun can sit before 'stare' ('mi sta chiamando') or attach to the gerund ('sta chiamandomi'). Same meaning.
'Avere bisogno' takes 'di'. 'Ne' stands in for that 'di' phrase, so 'ne ho bisogno' means I have need of it.
When a number stands alone without its noun, Italian still needs 'ne': 'ne prendo due', literally I take two of them.
